clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant subtype caused by mutations in COL1A1 (type 1/VIIA) or COL1A2 (type 2/VIIB) that cause skipping of exon 6, deleting the N-proteinase cleavage site of the proalpha chain of type I collagen.
The defining clinical feature is congenital bilateral hip dislocation together with severe generalised joint hypermobility and recurrent subluxations and dislocations.
Skin is hyperextensible with easy bruising and atrophic scarring, alongside muscle hypotonia, kyphoscoliosis and osteopenia.

It is the substrate-side mirror of dermatosparaxis: the same failure to remove the collagen N-propeptide, but caused by an abnormal collagen chain (dominant) rather than a deficient ADAMTS2 enzyme (recessive).
Collagen biochemistry from cultured fibroblasts shows retained pN-collagen (uncleaved proalpha chains).
Congenital hip dislocation may be misread as isolated developmental dysplasia; the accompanying hypermobility and skin findings are the clue.
Distinguish from Larsen syndrome, which also causes multiple congenital dislocations.
Management centres on joint protection and carefully planned orthopaedic care, as recurrent dislocation and early osteoarthritis dominate the course.
reference.pathophysiology: Arthrochalasia Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by heterozygous, usually dominantly acting mutations — most often splice-site variants that delete exon 6 — in COL1A1 (subtype 1, formerly VIIA) or COL1A2 (subtype 2, formerly VIIB). Exon 6 of these genes encodes the region of the amino-terminal propeptide that contains the recognition and cleavage site for procollagen I N-proteinase (ADAMTS2). When exon 6 is skipped, the N-propeptide cannot be removed, so pN-collagen persists and is incorporated into fibrils, disturbing fibril packing and markedly weakening ligaments, joint capsules and skin. The result is profound joint laxity with congenital hip dislocation and recurrent dislocations, skin hyperextensibility and fragility, hypotonia and reduced bone mass. Because the defect lies in the collagen substrate rather than the processing enzyme, inheritance is dominant, in contrast to the recessive, enzyme-deficient dermatosparaxis form that shares the same molecular endpoint.
additionalDifferentials: Other Ehlers-Danlos subtypes (classical, hypermobile and dermatosparaxis)
Isolated developmental dysplasia of the hip
Arthrogryposis and other congenital contracture syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of COL1A1 and COL1A2, targeting exon 6 splice variants
Biochemical collagen analysis of cultured fibroblasts showing uncleaved pN-collagen chains
Radiographs of the hips and spine for dislocation and kyphoscoliosis
Electron microscopy of skin for abnormal collagen fibrils
redFlags: Recurrent or irreducible major joint dislocations
Congenital bilateral hip dislocation requiring specialist management
Fragility fracture in the context of low bone mass
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is generally normal, but chronic joint instability, pain, recurrent dislocation and early osteoarthritis cause substantial disability, and hip reconstruction is complicated by fragile tissues and a tendency to re-dislocate.
pitfalls: Treating the congenital hip dislocation as isolated developmental dysplasia and missing the syndrome
Undertaking surgical stabilisation without allowing for fragile tissues and high re-dislocation rates
Confusing the picture with Larsen syndrome
Overlooking the skin fragility and atrophic scarring
management: No disease-specific therapy exists; centre care on physiotherapy and muscle strengthening to stabilise hypermobile joints and reduce dislocations
Manage recurrent dislocations and congenital hip dislocation with orthopaedic care, bracing and reconstructive surgery, anticipating fragile tissues and re-dislocation
Practise meticulous skin and wound care with careful suturing and support, given hyperextensible, fragile skin with atrophic scarring and easy bruising
Assess and manage reduced bone mass with bone densitometry, calcium and vitamin D optimisation and weight-bearing exercise, and treat kyphoscoliosis
Provide analgesia and multidisciplinary chronic-pain management with occupational therapy and mobility aids
Monitor for early osteoarthritis and progressive spinal deformity
Coordinate clinical genetics, orthopaedics and physiotherapy, and offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant COL1A1 or COL1A2 variants
